doc.title: Bob Hardaway interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: Composition study and choosing to be a player rather than a writer
summary: After more harmony study and composition at a private school on the G.I. Bill, he decided he lacked the talent of Mulligan, Al Cohn or Bill Holman to both write and play, and chose playing.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Indeed. But I wouldn’t have missed it for the world, having it taught to me like that. So I did that for a couple of years and then went to a private school called the American Operatic Laboratory, which I was studying composition there with a particular guy. I went there because this — he was approved by the Veterans. And there was a well known composer teaching there so I studied a bit with him. But actually I had to make a choice before I went there, because I didn’t feel I had enough talent to be a Gerry Mulligan, who could write and play, or an Al Cohn, who could write and play the way I like to write and play, or a handful of others, Bill Holman. And so I chose the playing. I decided I’d let the writing — forget it, and be a player. So that’s when I started really trying to apply myself to that.
It’s interesting because other fellows have had similar decisions, like you mentioned Bill Holman, and he went the other way.
Yeah. Well he had quite a good career of playing though too.
